quickTip: Longest-lasting SSRI: wait at least 5 weeks after the last dose before starting an MAOI, and watch patients under 25 for new suicidal thinking in the first months.
administration: Orally once daily in the morning, with or without food; a bedtime dose often keeps patients awake. Larger daily doses can be split between morning and noon.
mechanism: Inhibits the serotonin transporter on the presynaptic neuron; an active metabolite, norfluoxetine, keeps that block going for weeks after dosing ends.
simplified: The SSRI with a long tail: it keeps working, and keeps interacting, weeks after the last capsule.
nursing: Allow 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before an MAOI, and 14 days after stopping an MAOI before fluoxetine; never give with pimozide or thioridazine.
Hold and report fever, sweating, agitation, tremor, muscle jerking, or diarrhea after adding another serotonergic drug: possible serotonin syndrome.
Review the medication list: it strongly inhibits CYP2D6 and can raise levels of tricyclics, some antipsychotics, and some beta blockers.
Black box warning: assess mood and suicide risk at every contact in children, teens, and young adults, especially after dose changes.
Weigh regularly; appetite loss and weight loss can occur, which matters in patients treated for bulimia or who are underweight.

quickTip: Never pair it with citalopram (its parent drug) or an MAOI, and use caution with other QT-prolonging drugs; young patients need close suicide-risk monitoring early on.
administration: Orally once daily at the same time, morning or evening, with or without food. Tablets and an oral solution are available; the usual adult maximum is 20 mg a day.
mechanism: The purified active mirror-image half of citalopram; it binds the serotonin transporter very selectively, so serotonin stays in the synapse longer.
simplified: A precision SSRI: citalopram's working half, with few drug interactions.
nursing: Allow a 14-day gap before or after any MAOI, including linezolid and IV methylene blue.
Obtain an ECG and correct low potassium or magnesium in patients with heart disease or on other QT-prolonging drugs.
Explain that anxiety often eases in 1-2 weeks but mood takes 4-6 weeks; continue the drug and taper rather than stopping.
Black box warning: screen for worsening depression, agitation, or suicidal thoughts in patients under 25, especially in the first weeks.
Watch for bruising or bleeding when combined with aspirin, NSAIDs, or warfarin.

quickTip: Blood pressure rises with the dose, and a missed dose can bring on harsh discontinuation symptoms; check BP regularly and taper slowly over weeks.
administration: Extended-release capsules once daily with food at the same time; swallow whole or sprinkle the contents on applesauce without chewing. Immediate-release tablets are split into 2-3 doses with food.
mechanism: Blocks serotonin reuptake at lower doses and adds norepinephrine reuptake blockade as the dose climbs, boosting both signals in the synapse.
simplified: Two recycling pumps jammed at once: the extra norepinephrine is why blood pressure creeps up.
nursing: Measure BP at baseline and at each follow-up; report sustained readings above the patient's baseline, since the dose may need lowering.
Warn that stopping suddenly causes dizziness, electric-shock sensations, nausea, irritability, and flu-like feelings; its short half-life makes this worse than with fluoxetine.
Allow 7 days after stopping venlafaxine before starting an MAOI, and 14 days after an MAOI before venlafaxine.
Black box warning: monitor children, teens, and young adults for emerging suicidal thoughts or behavior.
Report eye pain or halos (angle-closure glaucoma) and check sodium in older adults.

quickTip: Lowers the seizure threshold: do not give to anyone with a seizure disorder, bulimia or anorexia, or who is abruptly stopping alcohol, benzodiazepines, or barbiturates.
administration: Swallow SR and XL tablets whole; crushing dumps the dose and raises seizure risk. Give XL in the morning; space twice-daily SR doses at least 8 hours apart with the last one well before bedtime.
mechanism: Blocks reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine with almost no effect on serotonin, raising alertness and motivation signals.
simplified: The antidepressant that skips serotonin: no weight gain or sexual side effects, but more jitters and a lower seizure threshold.
nursing: Screen for seizures, head injury, eating disorders, and heavy alcohol or sedative use before the first dose.
Wellbutrin and Zyban are the same drug; confirm the patient is not taking both, and never double up after a missed dose.
For smoking cessation, start 1-2 weeks before the quit date and watch for agitation, hostility, or depressed mood.
Black box warning: monitor young patients for suicidal thinking; allow 14 days between bupropion and an MAOI.
Check BP, especially when it is combined with nicotine patches, and teach to limit alcohol.

uses: Reducing suicidal behavior in schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder
quickTip: Agranulocytosis risk: baseline ANC must be at least 1,500/mcL, ANC is checked weekly for the first 6 months, and fever or sore throat needs same-day evaluation.
administration: Orally starting at 12.5 mg once or twice daily and increased slowly to limit fainting and seizures. If 2 or more days of doses are missed, restart at 12.5 mg rather than the prior dose.
mechanism: Weakly blocks dopamine D2 receptors while strongly blocking serotonin 5-HT2A and several other receptors, relieving psychosis that other drugs could not touch with very little EPS.
simplified: The last-resort antipsychotic that works when others fail, as long as the blood counts stay safe.
nursing: Follow the ANC schedule (weekly for 6 months, every 2 weeks to month 12, then monthly); hold and notify for ANC under 1,000/mcL or any sign of infection.
Report chest pain, resting tachycardia, fever, or shortness of breath in the first 2 months: possible myocarditis.
Start a bowel regimen and ask about stools every shift; untreated constipation can progress to fatal bowel obstruction.
Seizure risk climbs with dose; quitting smoking raises clozapine levels, so report any change in smoking habits.
Black box warning: increased death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis; also watch for NMS and protect the pillow from nighttime drooling.

quickTip: Among the highest risks for weight gain, high blood sugar, and high lipids: weigh the patient and check fasting glucose and lipids at baseline and regularly.
administration: Orally once daily with or without food; orally disintegrating tablets dissolve on the tongue. The long-acting pamoate injection requires at least 3 hours of observation afterward in a registered facility.

sideEffects.label: High blood sugar and new diabetes

mechanism: Blocks dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors; its strong histamine and muscarinic blockade explains the sedation, hunger, and anticholinergic effects.
simplified: Settles psychosis and mania well but switches on appetite, so the scale and glucose meter tell the story.
nursing: Record weight, BMI, and waist size, plus fasting glucose and lipids, before starting, at 12 weeks, and then periodically.
Teach signs of high glucose (thirst, frequent urination, fatigue) and encourage diet and activity from day one.
Do not give IM olanzapine together with an IM or IV benzodiazepine; dangerous cardiorespiratory depression can result.
After a long-acting injection, watch for post-injection delirium and sedation syndrome: confusion, slurred speech, and excessive sleepiness.
Black box warning: higher mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis; report fever with rigid muscles (NMS).

quickTip: Expect strong sedation and orthostatic dizziness during dose titration; it carries two black box warnings: dementia-related mortality and suicidality in young people.
administration: Immediate-release tablets usually twice daily, titrated upward over several days. Extended-release tablets once daily in the evening, swallowed whole, without food or with a light meal.
mechanism: Blocks dopamine D2 receptors loosely and briefly while firmly blocking serotonin 5-HT2A and histamine H1 receptors, so movement side effects are uncommon but drowsiness is prominent.
simplified: A light grip on dopamine and a heavy grip on histamine: few tremors, lots of yawns.
nursing: Take lying and standing BP during titration; have the patient sit on the bed edge before standing.
Monitor weight, fasting glucose, and lipids; in children and teens also track blood pressure, which can rise.
Arrange an eye exam for cataracts at the start of therapy and about every 6 months.
Avoid combining with other QT-prolonging drugs; ask about alcohol and other sedatives.
Taper rather than stopping suddenly, which can cause insomnia, nausea, and vomiting.

quickTip: Therapeutic level 4-12 mcg/mL. Black box warnings: test at-risk Asian patients for HLA-B*1502 before starting (SJS/TEN), and watch for aplastic anemia and agranulocytosis.
administration: Orally with meals; swallow extended-release tablets whole. Do not give the oral suspension at the same time as other liquid medicines, and avoid grapefruit juice, which raises levels.
mechanism: Binds voltage-gated sodium channels in their inactive state, preventing the rapid repetitive neuron firing that spreads a seizure or a neuralgia pain burst.
simplified: Holds the sodium gates shut between sparks, while revving up the liver so many drugs, itself included, clear faster.
nursing: Get CBC, liver enzymes, and sodium at baseline and periodically; hold and report fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, petechiae, or easy bruising.
It induces its own metabolism, so levels drop over the first few weeks; recheck levels and watch for ataxia and double vision (toxicity).
As a strong enzyme inducer it weakens oral contraceptives, warfarin, and many other drugs; teach a nonhormonal backup method since it causes neural tube defects.
Stop and report any rash immediately, especially in the first months of therapy.
Never stop abruptly; use fall precautions and check sodium if confusion or headache appears.

quickTip: Therapeutic level 50-100 mcg/mL. Black box warnings: liver failure, pancreatitis, and major birth defects such as neural tube defects.
administration: Orally with food to limit stomach upset; swallow delayed- and extended-release tablets whole and do not chew capsules. IV doses are diluted and infused over 60 minutes, no faster than 20 mg/min.
mechanism: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and T-type calcium channels and raises brain GABA levels, calming neurons through several routes at once.
simplified: A broad-spectrum seizure calmer whose cost falls on the liver, the pancreas, and an unborn baby.
nursing: Check liver enzymes at baseline and often during the first 6 months; report malaise, loss of appetite, vomiting, jaundice, or facial swelling.
Severe abdominal pain radiating to the back with vomiting needs amylase and lipase checked promptly: pancreatitis can be fatal.
Monitor platelets before surgery or dental work, and check ammonia if the patient becomes lethargic or confused.
Women who could become pregnant need effective contraception and folic acid; it is not used for migraine prevention in pregnancy.
It roughly doubles lamotrigine levels, and carbapenem antibiotics can drop valproate levels sharply; review every new drug.

quickTip: Black box warning: life-threatening rash such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, most likely when the dose is raised too fast or valproate is added; titrate slowly over weeks.
administration: Follow the starter-kit titration exactly, with or without food. Swallow XR tablets whole; place orally disintegrating tablets on the tongue; chewable dispersible tablets can be chewed or mixed in a little water.
mechanism: Blocks voltage-sensitive sodium channels and reduces glutamate release, steadying neurons that fire too easily.
simplified: Low and slow: a well-tolerated stabilizer whose one big danger is a rash from rushing the dose.
nursing: Teach to hold the dose and call right away for any rash, especially with fever, mouth sores, or swollen glands, most often 2-8 weeks in.
With valproate the lamotrigine dose is roughly halved; carbamazepine, phenytoin, and estrogen birth control lower its levels.
If doses stop for more than about 5 half-lives (roughly a week), restart the titration from the beginning instead of resuming the full dose.
Double-check the label: Lamictal is easily confused with Lamisil, lamivudine, and labetalol.
Taper over at least 2 weeks and monitor mood for depression or suicidal thoughts.

quickTip: Black box warning: with opioids it can cause fatal respiratory depression. Flumazenil reverses it, but diazepam outlasts the antidote, so sedation can return.
administration: IV undiluted, slowly (no faster than 5 mg/min) into a large vein; do not mix with other drugs or fluids. IM absorption is erratic. Rectal gel or nasal spray treats seizure clusters at home.
mechanism: Attaches to the benzodiazepine site on GABA-A receptors so each GABA signal opens the chloride channel more often, making neurons harder to fire.
simplified: The long-haul benzo: calms quickly and lingers for days, which smooths withdrawal but builds up in older adults.
nursing: During IV use, monitor RR, oxygen saturation, and BP, with bag-valve mask and suction ready.
After flumazenil, keep monitoring for resedation; the antidote can also trigger seizures in long-term benzodiazepine users.
Active metabolites last for days, so older adults accumulate the drug; it is on the Beers list and needs strict fall precautions.
Taper gradually after regular use; withdrawal (tremor, anxiety, seizures) may appear days after the last dose.
Teach caregivers how and when to give the rectal gel for a seizure cluster, and when to call 911.

quickTip: Its quick on-and-off action drives rebound anxiety between doses and high dependence risk; never stop it suddenly (withdrawal seizures) and never combine with opioids or alcohol.
administration: Immediate-release tablets usually 3 times daily; XR once daily, usually in the morning, swallowed whole. Discontinue only by a gradual taper, often no faster than 0.5 mg every 3 days.
mechanism: Enhances GABA-A receptor response to GABA; it is absorbed fast and cleared fast, so the calming effect rises and falls within hours.
simplified: Fast on, fast off: quick relief for panic, but the quick drop-off feeds cravings and rebound.
nursing: Assess for misuse, early refill requests, and use with alcohol or opioids; count and secure doses as a controlled substance.
Watch for withdrawal during any taper: insomnia, tremor, rebound panic, and seizures.
Ketoconazole and itraconazole are contraindicated; other CYP3A4 inhibitors such as clarithromycin and grapefruit also raise levels.
Check RR and level of sedation; flumazenil is the reversal agent for overdose.
Pair drug therapy with teaching on breathing techniques and counseling so the patient is not relying on the pill alone.

uses: Short-term insomnia with trouble falling asleep
quickTip: Black box warning: complex sleep behaviors (sleepwalking, sleep-driving) can injure or kill; take it right before bed with 7-8 hours left for sleep, and stop it after any episode.
administration: Orally immediately before bed, not with or right after a meal, which delays the effect. Starting dose is lower for women and older adults (5 mg immediate-release, 6.25 mg extended-release); swallow CR tablets whole.
mechanism: Binds selectively to the benzodiazepine site on GABA-A receptors that contain the alpha-1 subunit, producing sleep with little anti-anxiety, muscle-relaxing, or anticonvulsant effect.
simplified: A sleep-only GABA booster: it flips the brain into sleep mode but does nothing for anxiety or seizures.
nursing: Give only when the patient is in bed and ready to sleep; no driving or tasks needing full alertness the next morning.
Women clear it more slowly, so they and older adults get the lower dose; use night-time fall precautions.
Ask patients and bed partners about eating, driving, or walking with no memory of it; stop the drug if it happens.
No alcohol or other sedatives; flumazenil can reverse an overdose.
Intended for short-term use; reassess if insomnia persists beyond 7-10 days and warn of rebound insomnia when stopping.

quickTip: Relieves acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism, often within minutes by injection, but it does not treat tardive dyskinesia and can make it worse.
administration: Orally once daily at bedtime or in divided doses, with food if the stomach is upset. For an acute dystonic reaction, give 1-2 mg IM or IV as ordered.
mechanism: Blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the basal ganglia, restoring the dopamine-acetylcholine balance that antipsychotics tip toward acetylcholine.
simplified: Rebalances the seesaw: when dopamine is blocked, lowering acetylcholine eases the stiffness and spasms.
nursing: Assess for neck twisting, eyes rolling upward, tongue protrusion, and shuffling gait; reassess within 15-30 min after an injection.
It reduces sweating, so heatstroke is a risk: limit hot environments and strenuous exercise and encourage fluids.
Track urine output and bowel movements; report urinary retention, especially in older men with enlarged prostates.
Offer sugar-free gum or candy for dry mouth and a high-fiber diet; caution in glaucoma.
Watch for delirium when it is combined with other anticholinergic drugs such as antihistamines or tricyclics.

uses: Mild to moderate Parkinson disease dementia
quickTip: Remove yesterday's patch before applying today's and rotate sites; wearing more than one patch has caused overdoses with vomiting, slow heart rate, and collapse.
administration: Apply one patch daily to clean, dry, hairless skin on the upper or lower back, upper arm, or chest, not reusing a site for 14 days. Capsules are taken twice daily with breakfast and dinner, swallowed whole.
mechanism: Inhibits both acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine is broken down more slowly and memory circuits get a stronger signal.
simplified: Blocks two cleanup enzymes instead of one; the patch releases it gently to spare the stomach.
nursing: Label each patch with date, time, and initials; fold the removed patch sticky sides together and discard it out of reach of children and pets.
Check apical pulse before dosing and report a rate under 60, fainting, or dizziness, especially with beta blockers.
Weigh weekly; GI effects peak with dose increases and are stronger with capsules than the patch.
If more than 3 days of doses are missed, restart at the lowest strength to avoid severe vomiting.
Report black stools or worsening tremor in Parkinson patients.

uses: Severe chronic pain in opioid-tolerant patients (patch)
quickTip: Patches are only for opioid-tolerant patients; heat from fever, heating pads, or hot tubs speeds absorption to possibly fatal levels, and naloxone may need repeating.
administration: Patch on intact, hairless skin of the chest, back, flank, or upper arm; clip hair (do not shave), press for 30 seconds, and change every 72 hours. Full effect takes 12-24 hours. IV doses are pushed slowly.

sideEffects.label: Chest wall rigidity with rapid IV push

mechanism: A highly fat-soluble mu-opioid agonist, roughly 50-100 times more potent than morphine, that reaches the brain within minutes by IV or builds up slowly from a skin depot.
simplified: A tiny dose with huge power: it slips into the brain fast by IV or seeps in steadily from the skin for 3 days.
nursing: Confirm opioid tolerance (for example, at least 60 mg oral morphine daily for a week) before the first patch; never use it for acute or postoperative pain.
Keep heat sources off the patch and report fever; for slow shallow breathing, remove the patch, stimulate the patient, and give naloxone.
Drug keeps releasing from the skin for about a day after removal, so continue monitoring sedation and respirations.
Fold used patches sticky sides together and flush or use a take-back program; a discarded patch can kill a child or pet.
CYP3A4 inhibitors such as clarithromycin, ketoconazole, and ritonavir can push levels to fatal range; also start a bowel regimen.

quickTip: Roughly 5-7 times stronger than morphine milligram for milligram; mix-ups between hydromorphone and morphine, or with the high-potency concentration, have caused fatal overdoses.
administration: IV push slowly over at least 2-3 minutes; also given orally, subcut, IM, or by PCA. The high-potency 10 mg/mL product is only for opioid-tolerant patients.
mechanism: A semisynthetic relative of morphine that binds mu-opioid receptors in the brain and spinal cord with much greater strength per milligram.
simplified: Morphine's stronger cousin: small numbers on the syringe, big effect in the body.
nursing: Use an independent double-check with a second nurse for IV and PCA doses; confirm the drug name and concentration match the order.
Rate sedation with a scale before and 15-30 min after IV doses; increasing sleepiness is the warning sign before breathing slows.
For respiratory depression give naloxone in small titrated doses in patients on long-term opioids to avoid sudden withdrawal and pain crisis.
Pair every scheduled dose with a stimulant laxative and softener, and ask about the last bowel movement each shift.
Rise slowly and use fall precautions; no alcohol or other sedatives with any form, including extended-release tablets.

uses: Severe persistent pain needing around-the-clock opioid (extended-release)
quickTip: Never crush, chew, or split OxyContin, which releases 12 hours of drug at once; for combination tablets, keep total acetaminophen within the daily limit (4 g for healthy adults).
administration: Immediate-release tablets every 4-6 hours as needed. Extended-release tablets every 12 hours, one at a time with enough water to swallow right away; do not pre-soak, lick, or wet them first.
mechanism: A semisynthetic mu-opioid agonist that is well absorbed by mouth, with oral potency about 1.5 times that of oral morphine.
simplified: The oral workhorse opioid: the extended-release safety lock only works if the tablet stays whole.
nursing: Screen for misuse risk and check the prescription monitoring program; teach locked storage and take-back disposal.
Teach family to recognize overdose (pinpoint pupils, unresponsiveness, slow breathing) and use naloxone nasal spray at home.
Add up acetaminophen from every source, including OTC cold and sleep products, when a combination tablet is ordered.
Start a stool softener with a stimulant laxative and report no bowel movement in 3 days.
Avoid benzodiazepines and alcohol; CYP3A4 inhibitors such as erythromycin and azole antifungals raise oxycodone levels.

quickTip: Black box warnings for heart attack, stroke, and GI bleeding; take with food and a full glass of water, and never use around coronary bypass (CABG) surgery.
administration: Orally every 12 hours with food or milk and a full glass of water. OTC naproxen sodium is limited to 3 tablets (660 mg) in 24 hours unless a provider directs otherwise.
mechanism: Reversibly blocks both cyclooxygenase enzymes for about 12 hours, lowering the prostaglandins that sensitize pain nerves and inflame joints.
simplified: A longer-lasting ibuprofen: one dose covers half the day, so the stomach and kidneys are exposed longer too.
nursing: Report black stools, bloody vomit, or epigastric pain; risk climbs with age, steroids, anticoagulants, SSRIs, alcohol, and prior ulcers.
Monitor BP, weight, edema, BUN, and creatinine; it blunts diuretics and ACE inhibitors.
Teach not to add OTC ibuprofen or aspirin-containing products, which doubles the NSAID load.
Avoid in aspirin-sensitive asthma and late in pregnancy.
It raises lithium and methotrexate levels; watch for toxicity signs.

quickTip: Ask about sulfonamide allergy before the first dose; it is gentler on the stomach, but the black box heart attack, stroke, and GI bleeding warnings still apply.
administration: Orally once or twice daily, with food if the stomach is upset. Capsules can be opened and sprinkled on a spoonful of applesauce, taken right away with water.
mechanism: Selectively blocks COX-2, the enzyme switched on at sites of inflammation, while largely sparing the COX-1 that protects the stomach lining and helps platelets clump.
simplified: Aims at inflammation's COX-2 and mostly leaves the stomach's COX-1 alone, but tipping the clotting balance raises heart risk.
nursing: Screen for sulfonamide allergy and for asthma, hives, or reactions to aspirin or other NSAIDs.
It does not protect the heart like low-dose aspirin; patients prescribed aspirin continue it, knowing GI bleeding risk rises.
Monitor BP, weight, and renal function; avoid in severe heart failure and right around CABG surgery.
Teach stroke and heart attack warning signs: chest pain, shortness of breath, one-sided weakness, slurred speech.
Check INR with warfarin and levels with lithium, both of which it can raise.

uses: Upper GI bleeding and stress ulcer prevention (IV)
quickTip: The PPI most often given IV; months to years of use bring low magnesium (tremor, arrhythmias), fractures, and C. difficile, so step down when the reason for it ends.
administration: Delayed-release tablets once daily, typically before breakfast, swallowed whole without crushing or splitting; use granules in apple juice for feeding tubes. IV over about 2 minutes or as a 15-minute infusion.

sideEffects.label: B12 deficiency with years of use

mechanism: Activated in the acidic space of the parietal cell, it bonds tightly to the H+/K+ ATPase so that pump can no longer push acid into the stomach.
simplified: Switches off the stomach's acid pumps one at a time; only newly built pumps can restart acid.
nursing: Check magnesium before and during long-term use, especially with digoxin or diuretics; report cramps, tremor, or palpitations.
Report frequent watery stools that do not improve; send a C. difficile test as ordered.
Encourage calcium, vitamin D, and weight-bearing activity, and assess fall risk in older adults.
Preferred PPI with clopidogrel because it interferes least with clopidogrel activation.
Switch from IV to oral as soon as the patient can swallow; it can cause a false-positive urine THC screen.

uses: Prevention of chemotherapy and postoperative nausea
quickTip: Black box warning: tardive dyskinesia, which can be permanent; avoid use longer than 12 weeks and stop at the first involuntary face, tongue, or limb movements.
administration: Orally 30 minutes before meals and at bedtime. IV doses of 10 mg or less are pushed slowly over 1-2 minutes; larger doses are diluted and infused over at least 15 minutes.
mechanism: Blocks dopamine D2 receptors in the vomiting center and makes gut muscle more responsive to acetylcholine, so the stomach empties faster without extra acid.
simplified: Blocks dopamine to push the stomach forward and settle nausea, but the brain's movement centers feel it too.
nursing: Screen for abnormal movements at baseline and during therapy; older women and people with diabetes have the highest tardive dyskinesia risk.
Contraindicated with GI obstruction, perforation, or bleeding, pheochromocytoma, and seizure disorders.
Push IV doses slowly to prevent sudden anxiety and restlessness; keep diphenhydramine available for acute dystonia.
In diabetes, faster stomach emptying changes when food is absorbed; monitor glucose and adjust insulin timing as ordered.
Reduce the dose in kidney impairment and report new depression; avoid alcohol and other sedatives.

quickTip: Watch for extrapyramidal symptoms, especially acute dystonia and akathisia in children and young adults; treat with diphenhydramine or benztropine, and never use under age 2 or 20 lb.
administration: Orally, as a rectal suppository, deep IM into a large muscle, or IV no faster than 5 mg/min and never as a bolus. Avoid subcut injection and wear gloves, since the solution irritates skin.
mechanism: Blocks dopamine D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, with lesser histamine, muscarinic, and alpha-adrenergic blockade.
simplified: A low dose of an old antipsychotic that shuts the brain's nausea gate, with the same movement side effects.
nursing: Assess for jaw, neck, or eye spasms and inner restlessness after each dose, and keep diphenhydramine on hand.
Check BP after an injection and have the patient stay lying down briefly, then rise slowly.
Teach sunscreen and protective clothing, and caution against overheating since heat regulation is impaired.
Black box warning: increased mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis; report fever with muscle rigidity.
Avoid alcohol and other sedatives; no driving until the drowsiness is known.

uses: Prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting
quickTip: Place one patch behind the ear at least 4 hours before travel and wash hands well afterward, since drug rubbed into an eye dilates the pupil and blurs vision; avoid in angle-closure glaucoma.
administration: One patch on clean, dry, hairless skin behind one ear, left in place up to 3 days; replace behind the other ear if still needed. For surgery it goes on the evening before and comes off 24 hours after. Do not cut the patch.

sideEffects.label: Confusion and hallucinations in older adults

mechanism: Blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors along the inner-ear balance pathway and in the vomiting center, so motion signals do not set off nausea.
simplified: Mutes the inner ear's acetylcholine chatter so the motion message never reaches the vomiting center.
nursing: Screen for glaucoma, urinary retention or enlarged prostate, and bowel obstruction before applying.
Wash hands with soap and water after touching the patch, and wash the skin site after removal; fold the used patch sticky sides together.
Remove the patch before an MRI because its backing contains metal that can burn the skin.
After several days of use, dizziness, nausea, and headache can occur for a day or more after removal.
No driving or hazardous activity until the effect is known; report eye pain or seeing halos.

quickTip: Never give with calcium-containing IV solutions (lactated Ringer's, calcium gluconate, calcium-containing TPN) in neonates, since fatal precipitates can form in the lungs and kidneys.
administration: IV infusion over about 30 minutes, usually once or twice daily. For IM use, inject deep into a large muscle; when reconstituted with lidocaine to ease pain, that solution must never be given IV.
mechanism: Binds penicillin-binding proteins and halts cell wall cross-linking; it resists many beta-lactamases and crosses into the spinal fluid.
simplified: A once-a-day wall breaker that reaches the spinal fluid, which makes it a meningitis mainstay.
nursing: Ask exactly what happened with any penicillin reaction; a history of anaphylaxis needs provider review before the first dose, with epinephrine ready.
In children and adults, flush the line thoroughly with a compatible fluid between ceftriaxone and any calcium-containing solution, and never run them together.
Contraindicated in neonates with high bilirubin, since it displaces bilirubin from albumin.
Report right upper abdominal pain (gallbladder sludge) and check PT/INR in malnourished patients or those on warfarin.
After a single IM dose for gonorrhea, teach abstinence for 7 days and treatment of partners.

uses: Skin and soft tissue infections such as cellulitis
quickTip: Its side chain resembles amoxicillin's, so ask about penicillin allergy first; a history of anaphylaxis or hives to amoxicillin or ampicillin means hold and check with the provider.
administration: Orally every 6-12 hours with or without food (food eases stomach upset), spaced evenly. Shake the suspension, keep it refrigerated, and discard after 14 days.
mechanism: Blocks the enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan in the cell wall; first-generation drugs hit gram-positive staph and strep hardest.
simplified: The oral first-generation wall breaker aimed mostly at the skin's staph and strep.
nursing: Outline the edge of cellulitis with a skin marker and report redness spreading past the line or new fever; it does not cover MRSA.
Teach to finish every dose even after the skin or urine symptoms clear.
Report several watery or bloody stools a day, even weeks after the course ends.
Doses are reduced when creatinine clearance is low; check renal function in older adults.
It can cause a false-positive copper-reduction urine glucose test and a positive Coombs test.

uses: Diabetic foot and complicated skin infections
quickTip: It is a penicillin: confirm there is no penicillin allergy before the first dose, and remember each dose carries a sizable sodium load for heart failure and kidney patients.
administration: IV infusion over 30 minutes every 6-8 hours, or extended over 4 hours per hospital protocol. Give separately from aminoglycosides and flush between, because mixing inactivates the aminoglycoside.
mechanism: Piperacillin blocks cell wall cross-linking, including in Pseudomonas; tazobactam binds the beta-lactamase enzymes that would otherwise destroy piperacillin.
simplified: A wall breaker with a bodyguard: tazobactam disarms the bacterial enzyme that would chew up piperacillin.
nursing: Draw blood cultures before the first dose, then start it on time; observe the first infusion for hives, wheezing, or hypotension.
Track sodium, potassium, daily weight, and lung sounds in heart failure or kidney disease.
Monitor BUN and creatinine, especially in critically ill patients also receiving vancomycin.
Report 3 or more loose stools in 24 hours; test for C. difficile and do not give antidiarrheals.
Monitor for bleeding and check coagulation studies in patients with kidney failure or on long courses.

uses: Chlamydia and other sexually transmitted infections
COPD flares and sinus or ear infections
quickTip: Prolongs the QT interval and can trigger torsades de pointes: avoid with other QT-prolonging drugs, low potassium or magnesium, or known long QT.
administration: Orally once daily with or without food; the 5-day pack is 500 mg on day 1 then 250 mg daily. Do not take at the same time as aluminum or magnesium antacids. IV doses are diluted and infused over at least 60 minutes, never as a bolus or IM.

sideEffects.label: Hearing loss or ringing in ears

mechanism: Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and stops the growing protein chain from moving forward; it concentrates in tissues and has a very long half-life.
simplified: Jams the bacterial protein factory and lingers in tissue for days after the last pill.
nursing: Get a baseline ECG and potassium and magnesium in cardiac patients or those taking amiodarone, ondansetron, or haloperidol.
Report yellow skin, dark urine, or right upper abdominal pain, and any new hearing change.
Check the IV site for phlebitis and confirm the infusion concentration and time.
After a single 1 g dose for chlamydia, teach abstinence for 7 days and partner treatment.
Watch for worsening muscle weakness in myasthenia gravis and for watery diarrhea.

uses: Serious anaerobic infections such as lung abscess and intra-abdominal infection
Skin, bone, and joint infections, including some MRSA
quickTip: Black box warning: C. difficile diarrhea, which can start up to 2 months after the last dose; report frequent watery or bloody stools and avoid antidiarrheal drugs.
administration: Capsules with a full glass of water, staying upright to prevent esophageal ulcers. IV doses are always diluted and infused no faster than 30 mg/min, never pushed; single IM injections stay at 600 mg or less.
mechanism: Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocks peptide bond formation, which also shuts down toxin production by strep and staph.
simplified: Shuts the protein factory, toxin line included, but also wipes out the gut bacteria that keep C. diff in check.
nursing: Track stool number and consistency during therapy and for 2 months after; send a C. difficile test for 3 or more unformed stools in 24 hours.
With confirmed C. difficile, use contact precautions and soap-and-water handwashing, since alcohol gel does not kill spores.
Rapid IV infusion can cause hypotension and cardiac arrest; verify the dilution and rate on the pump.
Report rash, fever, or jaundice, and check liver and kidney function on long courses.
It enhances neuromuscular blocking agents, so monitor breathing closely after surgery.

drugClass: Sulfonamide and folate antagonist combination antibiotic
quickTip: Push fluids to prevent crystals in the urine and stop at the first rash, which can progress to Stevens-Johnson syndrome; the trimethoprim part also raises potassium.
administration: Orally, usually every 12 hours, with a full glass of water and 2-3 L of fluid a day unless restricted. IV doses are diluted and infused over 60-90 minutes, never by rapid infusion or bolus.

sideEffects.label: Crystals in urine and kidney injury

mechanism: Sulfamethoxazole blocks bacteria from using PABA to start folate, and trimethoprim blocks a later step, so bacteria cannot make the folate they need for DNA.
simplified: Two roadblocks on the same folate highway, so bacteria cannot build new DNA.
nursing: Ask about sulfa allergy; teach to stop and report rash, fever, sore throat, mouth sores, or blisters.
Monitor potassium and creatinine, especially in older adults or with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or spironolactone.
Teach sunscreen, protective clothing, and avoiding tanning beds.
It raises INR with warfarin and increases hypoglycemia risk with sulfonylureas; check INR and glucose more often.
Avoid in infants under 2 months and near term in pregnancy because of kernicterus risk; check CBC on long courses.

quickTip: Treats the bladder only; avoid it when creatinine clearance is low (the label cutoff is under 60 mL/min), and warn that rust-yellow to brown urine is expected and harmless.
administration: Orally with food or milk, which improves absorption and eases nausea; Macrobid is typically every 12 hours for 5-7 days. Avoid antacids containing magnesium trisilicate.

sideEffects.label: Cough, chest pain, and dyspnea (lung reaction)

mechanism: Bacterial enzymes convert it into reactive fragments that damage bacterial DNA and ribosomes; it concentrates in urine but barely reaches the blood.
simplified: A bladder-only drug that bacteria activate themselves, turning it into shrapnel that shreds their own DNA.
nursing: Check creatinine clearance before starting; with poor kidney function it fails to reach the urine and builds up toward toxic levels.
Teach to report fever, chills, cough, chest pain, or shortness of breath, which can appear within days; long-term use can cause lung fibrosis.
Stop and report numbness or tingling in the hands or feet, which signals peripheral neuropathy.
Not for kidney infections (pyelonephritis) because tissue levels are too low.
Avoid at term pregnancy, during labor, and in infants under 1 month because of hemolytic anemia risk.

quickTip: Space antacids, calcium, iron, zinc, magnesium, and multivitamins at least 2 hours before or after each dose, and stop at the first tendon pain (black box warning).
administration: Orally once daily with plenty of fluid; tablets with or without food, oral solution 1 hour before or 2 hours after eating. IV infused over 60 minutes (90 minutes for 750 mg), never rapidly or as a bolus.
mechanism: Traps DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV on cut bacterial DNA so replication stalls and the chromosome fragments; its spectrum covers typical and atypical pneumonia bacteria.
simplified: The respiratory fluoroquinolone: one daily dose reaches the lungs, the urine, and, unfortunately, the tendons.
nursing: Ask about tendon pain at every contact; risk is highest over age 60, with corticosteroids, and after kidney, heart, or lung transplant.
Black box warnings also cover peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, and myasthenia gravis flares; avoid in myasthenia gravis.
Obtain an ECG and correct potassium and magnesium in at-risk patients; avoid pairing with amiodarone or antipsychotics.
Check glucose often in diabetics on insulin or sulfonylureas; severe hypoglycemia has caused coma.
Reduce the dose when creatinine clearance is under 50 mL/min, and teach sunscreen and good hydration.
